No Eyes, No Problem: What Does Touch Contribute to Blind Baoding Ball Manipulation?

Ayush Deshmukh Affiliation: All authors are with the School of Informatics, University of Edinburgh, Edinburgh, UK. {a.deshmukh, n.agarwal-10}@sms.ed.ac.uk,{elle.miller, sethu.vijayakumar}@ed.ac.uk    Nalin Agarwal Affiliation: All authors are with the School of Informatics, University of Edinburgh, Edinburgh, UK. {a.deshmukh, n.agarwal-10}@sms.ed.ac.uk,{elle.miller, sethu.vijayakumar}@ed.ac.uk    Elle Miller Affiliation: All authors are with the School of Informatics, University of Edinburgh, Edinburgh, UK. {a.deshmukh, n.agarwal-10}@sms.ed.ac.uk,{elle.miller, sethu.vijayakumar}@ed.ac.uk    Sethu Vijayakumar ††thanks: *Equal contribution. Affiliation: All authors are with the School of Informatics, University of Edinburgh, Edinburgh, UK. {a.deshmukh, n.agarwal-10}@sms.ed.ac.uk,{elle.miller, sethu.vijayakumar}@ed.ac.uk
Abstract

Humans manipulate objects within their hands through touch alone with remarkable ease, but for robots, achieving sustained real-world manipulation without vision remains an open challenge. Although reinforcement learning (RL) can generate sophisticated blind manipulation policies in simulation, transferring them to a real dexterous hand remains hindered by continuously changing contacts, motion-induced tactile information drift, and the gap between simulated and physical dynamics. We study this problem through Baoding ball rotation on the Shadow Dexterous Hand Lite, using only proprioception and binary tactile feedback as observations. We achieve successful zero-shot transfer through a combination of a sensor-aligned, coupling-aware embodiment in simulation, tactile calibration, and two novel episodic domain randomisations: slew-rate action limits and STuck-AT Taxels. On the physical hand, the policy achieves sustained blind Baoding rotation, completing 225 consecutive 𝟏𝟖𝟎∘\mathbf{180^{\circ}} rotations (112.5 full rotations) at ∼0.36​rot/s\sim 0.36\;\text{rot/s} in a single continuous trial without any vision or object-state information. Furthermore, we evaluate the contribution of tactile sensing relative to proprioception alone and identify the hand regions where tactile information is most important. This is the strongest reported hardware result for Baoding ball manipulation in both rotation count and speed, irrespective of the sensing modality used. By effectively bridging the sim-to-real gap, our framework sets a new benchmark for sustained tactile-driven dexterous manipulation on physical hardware.

I INTRODUCTION

In-hand manipulation requires continuous control of contact, with fingers making, breaking, and re-establishing contact as the object moves relative to the hand. The hand is simultaneously the actuator and the sensor, so each corrective motion changes the contact state from which the next correction is made. This intermittent contact and discontinuous dynamics make in-hand manipulation difficult to model and control. Most approaches address this challenge by supplying object state externally, through cameras, markers, or privileged simulator information. These observations provide explicit information about object pose and geometry, yet humans can reorient objects in the hand without continuously observing them, relying instead on contact during manipulation. This raises a fundamental question: can contact alone stand in for explicit object state, as it does for humans?

We take this question literally. Unlike prior systems that rely on cameras [1, 2], motion-capture markers [3], or privileged simulator state distilled into a student policy [4, 5], our policy receives none of these; it observes only joint encoders and 16 binary contact signals, a representation shown to be sufficient in simulation for single-object rotation on hardware [6]. While most existing real-world in-hand manipulation studies focus on reorienting a single object via reinforcement learning (RL) [3, 7, 1, 6, 2, 5], we choose to study Baoding ball manipulation as a more challenging instance of in-hand dexterity: two objects circulate simultaneously, interact with each other as well as the fingers, and are manipulated here on only a four-fingered Shadow Dexterous Hand Lite. The phase relationship between the two objects must be maintained without being directly observed.

Prior approaches that attempt Baoding ball rotation have typically used external object-state information or tactile sensing to demonstrate rotation [8, 9, 10]. However, sustained zero-shot transfer of a blind policy from simulation to physical hardware remains an open challenge. More recently, dexterous Baoding ball rotation was demonstrated in simulation across multiple robotic hands using only proprioception and binary contacts [11]. It was shown that combining RL with self-supervision (e.g. latent multi-step forward dynamics) learned implicit representations of the manipulated object(s) state, which led to superhuman simulated blind dexterity [12]. Yet, these works did not provide any hardware results, so the transferability of these results was unknown.

In this work, we achieve zero-shot sim-to-real transfer of Baoding ball rotation using only proprioceptive and binary contacts as observations, extending upon the simulation results in [12, 11]. We construct a simulation embodiment that reproduces the physical tendon coupling and tactile sensor layout used on the Shadow Dexterous Hand Lite, and introduce per-channel tactile calibration, command slew-rate randomisation and Stuck-AT Taxels (STAT) to improve robustness to hardware discrepancies. We show that a policy trained entirely in simulation can complete 225 consecutive 180∘180^{\circ} rotations (112.5 full rotations) at ∼0.36​rot/s\sim 0.36\;\text{rot/s} in a single continuous trial on a physical Shadow Hand Lite from touch and proprioception alone. Our main contributions are as follows:

  • •

    A hardware-aligned Shadow Dexterous Hand Lite simulation with matched tactile sensor sites and action mapping that reproduces the physical tendon coupling.

  • •

    A per-channel hysteresis-based tactile calibration to mitigate sensor noise.

  • •

    Two episode-level randomisations, Slew-rate Domain Randomisation (SlewDR) and Stuck-AT Taxels (STAT), that encourage smoother policy outputs and reduce reliance on individual tactile channels.

  • •

    Rigorous benchmarking of Baoding ball rotation across increasing levels of feedback information and cumulative randomisation ablations.

  • •

    Zero-shot transfer of a blind Baoding policy to the Shadow Dexterous Hand Lite, sustaining rotation from proprioception and binary contact, with tactile feedback substantially improving performance and long-horizon recovery.

II Related Works

In-hand manipulation involves contacts that continuously form, break, and shift as the object moves relative to the hand. RL in simulation with domain randomization has made such skills practical, from block reorientation [3] and Rubik’s cube manipulation [13] on the Shadow Hand to agile cube reorientation on the Allegro Hand [1]. Later work generalized across object shapes and sensing modalities, using object pose and point clouds [4], a single depth camera [2], or vision combined with dense touch [14]. These methods obtain object state from outside the hand, even though the object is often occluded once the fingers enclose it.

Blind in-hand manipulation relies on the hand’s own sensing rather than external perception. Proprioception has enabled single-object rotation [5], and joint position and torque sensing has enabled sustained cube rotation and reorientation [7, 15]. However, light objects produce only small changes in the hand state [12], which motivates direct contact sensing. Dense and optical tactile representations provide richer contact information but are harder to simulate and calibrate [16, 17], whereas binary contacts are compact and transfer more readily [6, 18]. Existing blind hardware results with sustained manipulation involve a single object.

Baoding ball manipulation extends blind in-hand manipulation to the coordination of multiple free objects, requiring two balls to be coordinated through both ball–hand and ball–ball contacts, making it more challenging than single-object manipulation. Prior hardware results (Table II) rely largely on external object information. Nagabandi et al. [8] used stereo vision with model predictive control on a Shadow Hand, while Yuan et al. [9] fused depth point clouds with binary FSR sensing on an Allegro Hand. Blind hardware evidence remains limited. Yang et al. [10] estimated ball positions from a 653-taxel tactile array using a graph network, but reported only a single qualitative half-rotation on hardware. RoTO [12] and RoTO 2.0 [11] used binary tactile sensing, including on the Shadow Dexterous Hand Lite, but remain in simulation. Moreover, none of these hardware works demonstrates rapid rotation sustained over several minutes. We address this gap through zero-shot transfer of a blind policy to the Shadow Dexterous Hand Lite, using only proprioception and binary tactile sensing, and show sustained rotation on hardware.

III METHODOLOGY

III-A Problem Setting

The aim of this work is to record sustained Baoding ball rotations on the Shadow Dexterous Hand Lite through zero-shot sim-to-real transfer of an RL policy. Two identical smooth Baoding balls (1.581.58 inch in diameter, mass 5555 g) are rotated continuously through finger-based contacts, with the episode ending when a ball leaves the hand. We formulate the task as a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP) defined by the tuple (S,A,T,O,R,γ)(S,A,T,O,R,\gamma). We note here that the simulated transition dynamics TT is an idealisation of the real-world: the physical hand does not reach the same state under the same command because of the approximate tendon model, actuator dynamics, and hand–ball and ball–ball contact. Likewise, OO is idealized, since hardware proprioception carries calibration offsets, while the tactile channel exhibits latency and intermittent activations, so the same physical state can produce a different observation. A policy optimized under (T,O)(T,O) therefore is not guaranteed to reproduce that behaviour on hardware, which is the exact problem we seek to mitigate.

III-B Agent and Learning Setup

The agent is blind. Its observation consists of a four-frame stack, where each frame contains 52 proprioceptive values, comprising joint position, joint velocity, position error, and previous action for each of the 13 actuators, together with 16 binary tactile values, giving a 272-dimensional observation. No camera, depth, motion capture, or privileged state is available at inference. The action is a 13-dimensional joint-position command issued at 60 Hz. The same observation and action layout is used in simulation and on hardware. The hand is held at an approximately 15∘15^{\circ} tilt throughout, and the two balls are seated diagonally opposed at the start of every episode. We retain the reward from RoTO [12] unchanged, which consists of a dense term that encourages the hand to keep the balls from being dropped and the sparse term rewards a completed exchange when both balls reach their respective goal markers. Policies are trained with PPO in Isaac Lab using 10 s episodes, corresponding to 600 control steps.

III-C Hardware Platform and Sensing

The hardware system used in the study is a Shadow Dexterous Hand Lite with 16 kinematic joints (Figure 2). It comprises three fingers with three joints each and a four-joint thumb. The proximal interphalangeal (PIP) and distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints of the index, middle, and ring fingers are mechanically coupled, resulting in 13 independently commandable actuators.

The tactile sensing system uses twelve force-sensitive resistors (FSRs) distributed across the palm and phalanges, together with four BioTac sensors on the fingertips, at the DIP joints of the index, middle and ring fingers and at the thumb interphalangeal (IP) joint (Figure 2). The sites are chosen from per-link contact frequencies observed during a simulation run, with the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) regions having the highest frequency, followed by the PIP regions and the palm. The 16 tactile channels are converted into binary contact signals using a thresholding mechanism described in Section III-E4.

III-D Simulation Embodiment

We observed that the default coupling in the Isaac Lab Shadow Dexterous Hand asset is inconsistent with the coupling mechanism of the physical Shadow Dexterous Hand (Fig. 3). On hardware, the coupled joints move sequentially: during flexion, the PIP joint moves first while the DIP joint remains near zero until the PIP joint reaches approximately 100∘100^{\circ}, after which the DIP joint begins to move. During extension, the order is reversed, with the DIP joint returning before the PIP joint moves. In contrast, the default Isaac Lab asset models the DIP angle as a fixed multiple of the PIP angle, causing both joints to move simultaneously. Consequently, the default asset cannot be used directly as a hardware-aligned model.

We therefore implement the hardware coupling explicitly at each environment step. For each pair of coupled joints, the policy outputs a single command, and the command is applied sequentially according to the current joint configuration: during flexion, the PIP joint is actuated until the 100∘100^{\circ} coupling threshold is reached before the DIP joint is actuated, while during extension the order is reversed. For tactile sensing, small collision bodies are added at the sensor locations in simulation to match the coverage and location of the physical FSR sensors. Fig. 2 shows the physical hand with the FSR sensors alongside the corresponding simulated embodiment.

III-E Bridging the Sim-to-Real Gap

After aligning the simulated embodiment with the corrected sequential coupling and tactile sensing sites, residual gaps remain in the contact dynamics, joint motions and tactile thresholding. These are addressed by the following complementary methods, illustrated in Figure 4. We introduce Slew-rate Domain Randomisation (SlewDR) and Stuck-AT Taxels (STAT) to address these discrepancies, together with tactile calibration for zero-shot deployment on hardware.

III-E1 Physical Parameter Randomisation

Physical parameters are resampled at the start of each training episode to expose the policy to variation in ball and hand contact dynamics. Ball mass is sampled from 4545–100​g100\,\mathrm{g}, while static and dynamic friction are randomised independently across the balls and the distal, middle, proximal, knuckle, and palm regions of the hand. The friction ranges are selected to reflect the differing surface properties of these regions on the physical hand, with higher friction assigned to the distal segments to account for the silicone skin covering the BioTac fingertip sensors and lower values used for the smoother palm surface.

III-E2 Slew-rate Domain Randomisation (SlewDR)

Even with soft gains in simulation and equally low gains on the real hand, the policy still commanded joint motion faster than the hardware could execute. We suspect this is due to tendon friction and reflected motor inertia, which the simulated joint does not represent. We therefore apply a rate limit to actions at deployment, constraining the change in commanded position between consecutive steps. The same limit is applied in simulation as a randomisation, with the scale factor s∼𝒰⁡(0.3,1.0)s\sim\mathcal{U}(0.3,1.0) resampled at each episode reset. The published joint target is then

qtSR​-​des=qt+clip⁡(CLOSEqtdes−qt,OPEN−s​q˙max​Δ​t,s​q˙max​Δ​t),\begin{split}q^{\mathrm{SR\text{-}des}}_{t}=q_{t}+\operatorname{clip}\big(&q^{\mathrm{des}}_{t}-q_{t},\\ &-s\,\dot{q}^{\max}\Delta t,\;s\,\dot{q}^{\max}\Delta t\big),\end{split} (1)

where q˙max\dot{q}^{\max} is the rated joint velocity limit, Δ​t=1/60\Delta t=1/60 s, qdes,tq_{\mathrm{des},t} denotes the desired joint position and qtq_{t} denotes the joint-position command actually published to the robot. The same rate limit defined in Equation (1) is applied on hardware. Unlike in simulation, the scale factor ss is not resampled: it is held fixed throughout an episode and remains at the same value across every deployment episode. The values used are reported in the Section IV-A.

III-E3 Stuck-AT Taxels (STAT)

Policies trained on clean tactile input were found to over-rely on individual channels, which negatively impacted sim-to-real when these channels did not provide reliable readings. To counter this, we propose a novel domain randomisation technique called Stuck-AT Taxels. We corrupt the tactile channels during training, in the manner of dropout, so that no single channel can be treated as reliable. At each episode reset, a subset of kk of the twelve FSR channels is uniformly selected at random, and each selected channel ii is held at the fixed value viv_{i} for the whole episode, while the remaining channels report the true simulated contact state.

k∼𝒰⁡{0,…,6},vi∼𝒰⁡{0,1},k\sim\mathcal{U}\{0,\ldots,6\},\qquad v_{i}\sim\mathcal{U}\{0,1\}, (2)

III-E4 Tactile Calibration

We observed that using static FSR thresholds was insufficient for effective sim-to-real transfer, as the threshold value changed with the hands static pose, wire movement and the corresponding motion during deployment, even with no object in the hand. Thus, we converted each FSR channel into a binary contact value with 2 thresholds (high and low) to provide hysteresis:

τhi\displaystyle\tau^{\mathrm{hi}} =P99.5​(x)+5,\displaystyle=P_{99.5}(x)+5, (3)
τlo\displaystyle\tau^{\mathrm{lo}} ={med⁡(x)+2,if ​P99.5​(x)−med⁡(x)≤15,τhi−3,otherwise.\displaystyle=\begin{cases}\mathrm{med}(x)+2,&\text{if }P_{99.5}(x)-\mathrm{med}(x)\leq 15,\\[4.0pt] \tau^{\mathrm{hi}}-3,&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases} (4)

where P99.5​(x)P_{99.5}(x) is the 99.599.5th percentile and med⁡(x)\mathrm{med}(x) is the median of the robust baseline value calculated from empty-hand FSR readings before deployment. The additives +5+5, +2+2, and −3-3 are chosen empirically for this specific sensor layout. Binarization of the contact signal follows a Schmitt rule, it switches on above τhi\tau^{\mathrm{hi}} and switches off below τlo\tau^{\mathrm{lo}}, otherwise retains the previous timestep’s state.

IV Experimental Setup

IV-A Evaluation Protocol

We evaluated the trained policies on the physical Shadow Dexterous Hand Lite, mounted at approximately 15∘15^{\circ} downward from horizontal, with control commands issued at 60 Hz. The default proportional and derivative gains provided for the Shadow Dexterous hand Lite were scaled after testing by 0.150.15, except for the MCP flexion joints of the index, middle and ring fingers, which were kept at default, and the MCP abduction joints of the same three fingers, which were scaled by 0.30.3. These PD gains were kept fixed across all evaluated configurations.

All policies were deployed zero-shot, without hardware training, policy fine-tuning, or checkpoint selection based on hardware performance. The same pair of 1.581.58-in, 55-g Baoding balls was used across all hardware trials. For each configuration (Table I), 10 independent trials were performed, with the balls placed by hand before each trial and not disturbed thereafter. Trials ran until a ball left the hand, with no time limit imposed. The command slew scale ss was held fixed within and across trials, with s=0.65s=0.65 for the proprioception-only policy and s=0.53s=0.53 for all other policies. In simulation, each configuration was evaluated over 768 episodes using 256 parallel environments and three training seeds. Episodes were limited to 10 s, with policy control at 60 Hz and physics simulation at 240 Hz. The evaluation used the same balls with the same initial-position perturbation (±5\pm 5 mm spawn noise) to ensure that none of the evaluation environments were fully deterministic.

IV-B Evaluation Metrics

IV-B1 Real-world Metrics

  • •

    Full Rotations: the total number of complete 360∘360^{\circ} rotations completed before a ball leaves the hand. A full rotation consists of two consecutive successful ball exchanges. Each exchange transfers the pair of balls around the hand and swaps their relative positions; after two exchanges, the pair returns to its original relative configuration, corresponding to one complete 360∘360^{\circ} rotation.

  • •

    Time-to-drop (tdropt_{\mathrm{drop}}): the elapsed time from the the moment both balls are seated in the hand until either ball leaves the hand.

  • •

    Rotational speed: the rate of rotation R10/min⁡(10,tdrop)R_{10}/\min(10,t_{\mathrm{drop}}) (rot/s), where R10R_{10} is the number of complete rotations within the first 10​s10~s.

  • •

    Exchange efficiency (η\eta): the fraction of executed gait cycles that result in a completed ball exchange, computed as

    η=2​R10fgait​T,\eta=\frac{2R_{10}}{f_{\mathrm{gait}}T}, (5)

    where fgaitf_{\mathrm{gait}} is the gait frequency measured from the joint trace and T=min⁡(10,tdrop)T=\min(10,t_{\mathrm{drop}}). Since at most one exchange can occur per gait cycle, η≤1\eta\leq 1.

IV-B2 Simulation-to-real Metrics

Simulation episodes are limited to 10 s. We therefore compare domains using rotational speed over the same early window: R10/min⁡(10,tsurv)R_{10}/\min(10,t_{\mathrm{surv}}) in simulation, where tsurvt_{\mathrm{surv}} is episode survival time in seconds. Alongside it we report the Drop Rate, the fraction of episodes in which either ball leaves the hand within the 10 s.

For each configuration, hardware results are reported as mean ±\pm standard deviation over 10 trials. Simulation results are aggregated over 768 episodes across three training seeds.

V Results

V-A Real-world Performance

The evaluated configurations and their corresponding training randomization and feedback settings are summarized in Table I. The C3 policy leads on all three metrics, achieving 34.75±26.0634.75\pm 26.06 full rotations, a time-to-drop of 94.8±68.094.8\pm 68.0 s, and a rotation speed of 0.360±0.0610.360\pm 0.061 across 10 trials. All trials reached at least two full rotations, and 9/10 continued beyond the 10-s window. Removing tactile feedback from the same policy in C3-TacOff reduced performance from 34.75 to 5.00 full rotations and from 94.8 s to 19.0 time-to-drop, while the corresponding decrement in rotation speed was smaller, from 0.36 to 0.256. The separately trained proprioception-only policy achieved 4.40 rotations compared with 1.70 for open-loop replay, while its performance was close to C3-TacOff (4.40 vs. 5.00 rotations).

The effect of the cumulative randomization stack is evaluated through the C1–C3 ladder as shown in Table II. C3 substantially outperforms the two intermediate configurations across all reported hardware metrics. C1 and C2 both fail to sustain the task on hardware (Table II), with median performance of 0.00 and 0.50 full rotations and median times-to-drop below 6 s. The transition from C1 to C2 provides no measurable gain: full rotations increase only from 0.35 to 0.50 with overlapping ranges, while time-to-drop decreases from 5.9 to 4.1 s. C3, by contrast, increases from 0.50 to 34.75 full rotations and from 4.1 to 94.8 s in time-to-drop relative to C2. The low variance of C1 and C2 reflects consistent failure.

V-B Simulation-to-real Comparison

The simulation and hardware results for the common evaluation metrics and the randomization ladder are shown in Table II. C3 and C3-TacOff show the closest simulation-to-hardware agreement among all configurations in terms of rotation speed.

V-C Long-Horizon Demonstration

A separate deployment of the C3 policy completed 112.5 full 360∘360^{\circ} rotations in 310 seconds. The run used the same checkpoint and deployment conditions as the 10-trial evaluation, but was conducted outside that set and is therefore not included in the reported statistics.

VI Discussion

VI-A What is tactile providing?

We evaluate four policies on hardware under different feedback conditions: open-loop replay, proprioception-only, C3-TacOff, and C3. Open-loop. Open-loop replay was the least robust condition (Table II), as the fixed trajectory cannot adapt and is highly sensitive to the initial ball configuration. Proprioception-only. The separately trained proprioception-only policy produced the results shown in Table II. It exhibited one of the fastest gaits among the four conditions while achieving one of the lowest exchange efficiencies. This mismatch between fast motion and low efficiency suggests that a faster gait does not necessarily result in more successful rotations. Removing the balls had little qualitative effect on the policy behaviour, as shown in Fig. 5, where the joint trajectories remain largely unchanged across gait cycles with and without the balls. Similar behaviour was observed when the position-error and velocity inputs were zeroed in simulation. These observations suggest that the policy primarily executes a repeated learned cycle rather than continuously adapting its motion to the instantaneous object configuration, consistent with its low exchange efficiency.

C3-TacOff. We use the C3 checkpoint with tactile observations zeroed at deployment. C3-TacOff achieved the results shown in Table II, with performance very similar to the separately trained proprioception-only policy across the evaluated hardware metrics. It maintained a similar gait frequency to C3, completing approximately 8.1 versus 7.9 cycles, but with substantially lower exchange efficiency. Qualitatively, C3-TacOff exhibited a repeated gait similar to the proprioception-only policy, with balls moving between neighbouring fingers until aligned for exchange. Its gait speed was also similar between simulation and hardware, while the simulation drop rate was significantly higher when tactile feedback was removed. This suggests that C3-TacOff retains the learned gait but loses the tactile-based corrections needed to sustain the manipulation.

C3. With tactile input restored, C3 achieved the results shown in Table II. The exchange efficiency of η=0.90\eta=0.90 is close to the theoretical upper bound of one exchange per gait cycle. Compared to C3-TacOff the difference in sustained performance is substantial: C3 achieved approximately 7×7\times as many rotations as C3-TacOff and remained active for nearly 5×5\times as long before dropping. This difference in motion adaptation can also be seen in Fig. 5. The joint trajectories of C3 show greater variation across gait cycles, with varying peak amplitudes and secondary peaks, whereas proprioception-only and C3-TacOff remain more repetitive. This indicates that C3 adjusts its motion across cycles rather than simply repeating the nominal gait. Comparing C3 and C3-TacOff in simulation, the drop rate decreases from 32% to approximately 2% with tactile input. This is consistent with the behaviour observed on hardware, where tactile feedback enables recovery from unfavorable ball configurations. In one observed recovery, the thumb initially failed to push one ball sufficiently toward the ring finger and instead retained the incoming ball, while the index and middle fingers repositioned the other ball. Once the required configuration was reached, the learned gait resumed.

Taken together, these results suggest two complementary roles for tactile feedback during in-hand Baoding ball rotation. First, tactile feedback improves exchange completion, allowing a larger fraction of the executed gait cycles to result in successful exchanges. Although the learned gait can be executed without tactile feedback, many of these cycles do not lead to a successful exchange. Second, tactile feedback improves task sustainment by allowing the policy to recover from unfavorable ball configurations. When the balls deviate from the configuration required by the nominal gait, tactile feedback enables the policy to adjust its motion and restore the intended configuration to continue the manipulation.

VI-B How do these randomization enable transfer?

C1 performs the worst on hardware despite the best simulation performance (Table II). The simulated gait approaches one rotation per second, but this aggressive motion does not transfer to hardware, where execution is substantially slower and difficult to sustain. The difference is also visible in Fig. 2, where the simulated actions are larger and more rapid than those observed on hardware.

C2 introduces slew-rate randomization during simulation. The rate limit caps the change in commanded joint position at each step, so large policy outputs cannot produce equally large instantaneous motions. The policy therefore learns to avoid abrupt commands and produce smoother motion that is easier for the hardware to track, as shown in Fig. 7, resulting in an increase in the mean number of rotations on hardware compared with C1 (Table II). The simulated gait speed also drops substantially, reaching the lowest speed among the evaluated configurations, while the simulation and hardware speeds are correspondingly closer. However, introducing a range of slew rates makes the RL problem substantially harder, as reflected by the drop in reward across the three training seeds in Fig. 6. Although the motion transfers more closely to hardware, all hardware trials still ended in a drop.

Addition of STAT. STAT combines the smoother motion of C2 with substantially greater robustness, outperforming all previous policies across every measured hardware metric, as shown in Table II. The remaining performance gap in C2 can be traced directly to its reliance on tactile feedback: when tactile input is removed from C2 in simulation, the drop rate rises to nearly 60%, indicating that, despite its smoother gait, the policy remains heavily dependent on continuous tactile feedback to sustain the manipulation. STAT is trained specifically to reduce this dependence. When tactile observations are removed from the STAT-trained policy, the drop rate increases from 2.2% to 32.2%, substantially less than the degradation observed for C2, while the underlying motion remains active. This behaviour is consistent with the proprioception-only policy, which can execute the nominal gait without tactile feedback, albeit with substantially lower robustness. Together, these results clarify the role of the randomization introduced by STAT. Rather than relying on tactile feedback to generate motion, STAT shifts the primary burden of execution onto the learned gait itself, with tactile feedback serving a supporting role in local adjustment and correction. The policy therefore uses the learned gait as the primary driver of motion, while using tactile feedback to correct deviations in the ball configuration, rather than relying on it continuously to sustain the motion.

VI-C How much tactile information is needed?

The spatial mismatch shown in figure  8 indicates that successful transfer does not require an exact sensor-wise correspondence between the simulated and physical tactile locations for this particular task. The policy appears to benefit from sparse information from these tactile channels. The sparse nature of the tactile signal also makes binary sensing important, thus each FSR was calibrated against its empty-hand baseline before deployment using the hysteresis-based thresholding procedure described in Section III-E4. We additionally investigated a motion-relevant calibration technique to account for changes in baseline values during hand motion which did not consistently improve transfer and was not retained in the final procedure.

The spatial sparsity of tactile observations in simulation and hardware motivated the use of episodic STAT. Since only a small number of channels is strongly activated, dependence on any individual channel could make the policy sensitive to sensor faults or shifts in contact density. Randomly corrupting a subset of channels encourages the policy to remain functional even if some channels are unavailable for contact information.

VII CONCLUSIONS

We demonstrated zero-shot sim-to-real transfer of blind Baoding ball rotation on the Shadow Dexterous Hand Lite using only proprioception and binary tactile contact without vision or any object-state estimation. Hardware-aligned coupling and sensor sites, motion-relevant tactile calibration, and episode-level SlewDR and STAT bring the simulation close enough to sustain rotation on the physical robot, including a long-horizon demonstration of 225 consecutive 180∘180^{\circ} exchanges. It is observed that the policy retains a rhythmic proprioceptive motion prior that continues without tactile input, while binary contact steers that prior into completed rotations and recovery. Open-loop replay, proprioception-only, and C3-TacOff ablations support this separation of roles and explain why removing touch collapses performance. Looking ahead, we aim to generalise across different ball sizes and masses, move beyond spherical objects to irregular shapes, and test denser or continuous tactile sensing under the same blind, zero-shot transfer setting.
